summary: Explores why protocols need their extension and version-negotiation mechanisms to be used regularly. If a mechanism is never exercised, implementations tend to get it wrong and later changes become hard or costly. The document gives examples where lack of use made evolution difficult. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Protocol extensions work only if implementations keep using and testing them. RFC 9170 explains how regular use can uncover compatibility problems before a new feature depends on a mechanism that has gone untested.

questions: what is active use of protocol extensions
subtitle: Why protocols need regular real-world use of their extension mechanisms.

tldr.problem: An extension or version-negotiation mechanism can be carefully designed and still fail if implementations rarely use it. Bugs or assumptions about unknown values may remain hidden until a protocol change is needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends active use of extension mechanisms and new values, especially when handling them is necessary for normal operation. It also discusses GREASE and other practices that can help reveal intolerance.
tldr.outcome: This Informational IAB document explains lessons from protocol deployments and offers design guidance. It does not define a new protocol mechanism.

today: RFC 9170 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board that offers guidance on protocol evolution. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Protocols Need to Change
sections.content:
Protocols need to adapt as user needs and deployment conditions change. An extension point allows a protocol to add or modify features, while version negotiation helps participants choose a version they can use together.

The RFC explains that defining an extension mechanism does not guarantee that it will work in practice. Implementations need to handle it correctly, and deployments need to exercise it while problems can still be found and fixed.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols need ways to add features as needs change. Those mechanisms must be used in real deployments to show that implementations can handle them.

sections.title: How Disuse Causes Failures
sections.content:
When extension mechanisms are rarely used, implementation errors can remain unnoticed. Years later, an attempt to add a feature may expose those errors across many implementations, making the change difficult to deploy. Middleboxes and other participants can also affect whether new values reach their destination.

The RFC gives examples from Internet protocols. IPv6 could not rely on the IP version field for selection over Ethernet, and new values in TLS and DNS have encountered intolerance. The problem is not limited to an endpoint pair: every system that handles or relays protocol data can affect a change.
sections.plainLanguage: If implementations rarely see new values, they may fail when a real extension arrives. The more systems involved in a protocol exchange, the more places a new feature may encounter problems.

sections.title: Keep Extension Mechanisms in Active Use
sections.content:
Active use means specifying, implementing, and deploying features that rely on an extension mechanism. Mechanisms are more likely to remain usable when deployments repeatedly encounter new extensions and unknown values. A protocol can encourage this by making extension handling important to normal operation, as SMTP does for message headers.

GREASE is one way to exercise negotiation points: an endpoint offers reserved values that have no assigned meaning, to test whether peers tolerate unfamiliar options. The RFC cautions that this approach tests only some behaviors and is not suitable for every extension design. Protocol designers should also ensure that implementations can report errors so problems surface early.
sections.plainLanguage: Use extension mechanisms throughout a protocol's life, not only when a major change is needed. Testing with unfamiliar values can reveal some errors, but it does not replace real use or effective feedback.

sections.title: Additional Design Practices
sections.content:
The RFC describes complementary practices that can make active use more effective. A smaller number of broadly useful extension points can receive more consistent use. Documenting protocol invariants helps clarify which properties should remain stable as other parts change.

Encryption and integrity protection can limit the ability of middleboxes to inspect or alter protocol traffic, although authorized participants can still affect extensibility. Feedback systems help developers detect deployment errors, especially during early use of a change. These techniques support protocol evolution but do not guarantee it on their own.
sections.plainLanguage: Clear invariants, fewer broadly useful extension points, and useful error reports can support protocol change. These practices help, but active and repeated use remains important.
